column2: Quick. What's eighty-five squared?
Seven thousand two hundred twenty-five. Eight times nine is seventy-two. Then write twenty-five.
If that took you longer than four seconds, here's why. School teaches multiplying on paper. For this one, that's two rows of digits and three carries, built up from the small end.
On paper that's fine, because the paper remembers the rows. In your head, you have to hold them all at once.
The trick holds one number. Seventy-two.
And it rests on a picture. If you ever forget the trick, the picture gives it back. So every trick in this video comes with its picture, and with a few problems for you to try.
Here's that trick on a smaller number. Thirty-five squared. Look at the number in front of the five. Three.
Multiply it by the next number up. Three times four is twelve.
Then write twenty-five after it. One thousand two hundred twenty-five.
But why the next number up? Why three times four, and not three times three?
Thirty-five squared is the area of a square, thirty-five on each side. Cut each side into thirty and five.
The big block is thirty by thirty. The little corner is five by five. That's the twenty-five.
That leaves two strips, each thirty long and five wide. Slide one of them round, next to the other.
Side by side, they're ten wide. So the block has grown from thirty by thirty to thirty by forty. Three times four, in hundreds.
That's where the next number comes from. The two fives make one more ten.
Your turn. Whenever you want more time, pause the video. What's twenty-five squared?
Two times three is six. Then twenty-five. Six hundred twenty-five.
Sixty-five squared?
Six times seven is forty-two. Then twenty-five. Four thousand two hundred twenty-five.
Now past a hundred, where the number in front is ten. What's a hundred and five squared?
Ten times eleven is a hundred and ten. Then twenty-five. Eleven thousand and twenty-five.
It works for every whole number that ends in five. If the number in front is n, the square is n, times n plus one, in hundreds. Plus twenty-five.
It is only as easy as that one multiplication. A hundred thirty-five squared needs thirteen times fourteen. For that, we need a way to multiply any two numbers.
Twenty-three times forty-six. No fives to help. Before anything else, ask how big the answer should be. Twenty times fifty is a thousand. So, somewhere near a thousand.
Now draw it. A rectangle, twenty-three by forty-six. Its area is the answer.
Break each number into parts. Twenty and three. Forty and six. The rectangle falls into four pieces.
Take the big piece, twenty by forty. Two times four is eight. But eight what? Eighty, eight hundred, or eight thousand?
Eight hundred. Twenty times four is eighty already, so twenty times forty has to be ten times that. Tens times tens are hundreds.
So leave the zeros out while you multiply. Then put them back by asking how big the piece has to be.
The other three go the same way. Twenty times six, a hundred twenty. Three times forty, a hundred twenty. Three times six, eighteen.
Four easy multiplications. What's left is adding them up. And that's the part that goes wrong.
Four numbers is a lot to hold while you're still multiplying. So don't hold them. Keep one running total, and add each piece the moment you have it.
Start with the big piece. Eight hundred. Add a hundred twenty. Nine hundred twenty. Another hundred twenty. One thousand forty. And eighteen. One thousand fifty-eight.
You only ever held one number. And the first thing you said, eight hundred, was already in the right neighbourhood.
Your turn. Six times forty-three?
Six forties are two hundred forty. Six threes are eighteen. Two hundred fifty-eight.
And the one we left. Thirteen times fourteen?
A hundred. A hundred forty. A hundred seventy. A hundred eighty-two. So a hundred thirty-five squared is eighteen thousand two hundred twenty-five.
Forty-seven times fifty-three. Before you start on the parts, look at the two numbers. What do they have in common?
They're the same distance from fifty. Three below, and three above.
So draw fifty squared, and lay the rectangle over it. It sticks out by three on one side, and falls short by three on the other.
Move the part that sticks out into the gap. It nearly fills it. What's missing is one small square, three by three.
So the answer is fifty squared, minus three squared. Twenty-five hundred, minus nine. Two thousand four hundred ninety-one.
Your turn. Nineteen times twenty-one?
The middle is twenty, and they're one away. Four hundred, minus one. Three hundred ninety-nine.
Sixty-five times seventy-five?
The middle is seventy. Five away. Forty-nine hundred, minus twenty-five. Four thousand eight hundred seventy-five.
It needs a middle that's easy to square. Forty-seven times fifty-six has its middle at fifty-one and a half. Back to parts.
The next trick comes with a story. Los Alamos, in the nineteen forties. Richard Feynman is working under Hans Bethe, and they're putting numbers into a formula. They get to forty-eight squared.
Feynman reaches for the calculator, a mechanical one. Bethe says, that's twenty-three hundred.
Feynman starts pushing the buttons anyway. And Bethe says that if he wants it exactly, it's twenty-three oh four.
Feynman is impressed. And Bethe asks him a question. Don't you know how to square numbers near fifty?
Fifty squared is twenty-five hundred. How would you get from there to forty-eight squared?
Bethe's way. Forty-eight is two below fifty, so take two hundred off. That's his twenty-three hundred. Then add two squared. Twenty-three oh four.
Here's why that works. Forty-eight squared sits inside fifty squared. To cut down to it, take a strip off the top and a strip off the side. Each strip is fifty by two. A hundred each.
But the two strips cross in the corner. That small square, two by two, got taken off twice. So one of them goes back. Plus four.
Now a number above fifty. What changes for fifty-three squared?
The same picture, with the strips put on. Two strips, fifty by three. Lay them end to end and they're a hundred by three. Three hundreds. And this time the corner is new. Three by three. Nine.
So fifty-three squared is twenty-five hundred, plus three hundred, plus nine. Two thousand eight hundred nine.
Which gives a quick way to say it. Start from twenty-five. Add the distance from fifty, or take it off. That's the hundreds. Then write the distance squared.
Your turn. Fifty-two squared?
Twenty-five plus two is twenty-seven. Two squared is four. Twenty-seven oh four.
Forty-six squared?
Four below. Twenty-five minus four is twenty-one. Four squared is sixteen. Twenty-one sixteen.
Fifty-seven squared?
Seven above. Thirty-two. Seven squared is forty-nine. Thirty-two forty-nine.
That reads straight off while you're within nine of fifty. Further out, the square spills over into the hundreds. Sixty-two squared is thirty-seven hundred, plus a hundred forty-four.
Feynman says he took up tricks like this himself after that. He writes that he very rarely beat Bethe to an answer. And he says why. Every number was near something Bethe knew.
Now money. A forty-eight dollar bill, and you want to leave fifteen percent. Ten percent is easy. The decimal point moves one place. Four dollars eighty.
Five percent is half of that. Two forty. Together, seven dollars twenty.

Turn it round. Twenty-five percent of eight is a quarter of eight. Two. And eight percent of twenty-five is also two.
Percent means per hundred. So both are eight times twenty-five, over a hundred. The same rectangle, turned on its side.
Your turn. Four percent of seventy-five?
Seventy-five percent of four. Three quarters of four is three. The swap only pays when one of the two is a friendly percent.
Some numbers are one step from a round one. Five is half of ten. So five times eighty-six is ten times eighty-six, cut in half. Eight sixty, halved. Four hundred thirty.
The same cut works between two numbers. Fourteen times thirty-five. Halve the fourteen, double the thirty-five. Seven times seventy. Four hundred ninety.
Nine is one short of ten. So nine times thirty-seven is ten of them, less one. Three seventy, minus thirty-seven. Three hundred thirty-three.
Prices are built for this. Four things at nineteen ninety-nine. Call it four twenties. Eighty dollars. Then give back four cents. Seventy-nine ninety-six.

Now they're mixed up, so the first job is to pick the trick. Pause whenever you like. Seventy-five squared?
It ends in five. Seven times eight is fifty-six. Five thousand six hundred twenty-five.

One either side of fifty. Twenty-five hundred, minus one. Two thousand four hundred ninety-nine.

Near fifty. Twenty-nine. Then sixteen. Twenty-nine sixteen.

Nothing to grab. No five, no easy middle, no round number next door. Parts still works. Forty-two hundred. Forty-six eighty. Fifty-one seventy. Fifty-two twenty-six.
That's four pieces with carrying, and it's slow. There's no shame in reaching for paper, or a calculator. That's what they're for.
But keep one habit even then. Round first. Seventy times eighty is fifty-six hundred. So if the screen says five hundred, or fifty thousand, you know something went wrong.
Look back at three of the pictures. Thirty-five squared. Forty-eight squared. Forty-seven times fifty-three. What did they share?

One move. Slide a strip from one side of a square to the other, and you're left with an easy rectangle and a small square. Thirty times forty, plus twenty-five. Forty-six times fifty, plus four. Fifty squared, minus nine.
None of this is new. An American school book from eighteen forty-four has the fives trick, the middle trick and the near fifty trick, all on one page.
And none of it takes a gift. It takes a few numbers you know well, and the habit of looking for the nearest one. Every number is near something you know.
